srcs: Living with excessive sweating, or hyperhidrosis, can be frustrating and sometimes embarrassing. While we understand it's a sensitive topic, open communication with your healthcare provider is key to finding the best treatment plan for you. Sometimes, patients may hesitate to share all their symptoms or lifestyle factors due to various reasons. We want to assure you that our primary goal is to help you feel comfortable and confident in your skin.
Here are a few things to consider when discussing your sweating concerns with your doctor:

Honesty is the best policy: While it might feel awkward to discuss certain details, your doctor needs a complete picture of your symptoms, including when and where you sweat most, triggers, and how it affects your daily life. This information helps them determine the underlying cause and tailor treatment options specifically for you.

Lifestyle factors matter:  Your daily habits, including diet, exercise, and stress levels, can play a role in sweating. Be open about your lifestyle choices, as simple modifications can sometimes make a significant difference.

Don't hold back on concerns:  If you have any worries or questions about potential treatments or side effects, please don't hesitate to voice them. Your doctor is there to address your concerns and work with you to find a solution that fits your needs and preferences.

Remember, you're not alone: Hyperhidrosis is a common condition affecting many people. Sharing your experiences and concerns with your doctor can empower you to take control of your sweating and improve your quality of life.

We encourage you to schedule a follow-up appointment with Dr. Anika Sharma to discuss your recent lab results and any other concerns you may have. Together, we can work towards finding effective solutions and helping you feel your best.
trgs: Kozala na bokono ya kotoka mingi, to hyperhidrosis, ekoki kopesa nkanda mpe ntango mosusu nsoni. Atako toyebi ete ezali likambo ya mpasi, kosolola polele na monganga na yo ezali nzela ya malamu mpo na kozwa bankisi oyo ebongi na yo. Ntango mosusu, bato ya maladi bakoki kokakatana koyebisa bilembo na bango nyonso to ndenge bafandaka mpo na bantina ndenge na ndenge. Tolingi koyebisa yo ete mokano na biso ya liboso ezali ya kosalisa yo oyoka malamu mpe ozala na kondima na nzoto na yo.
Talá makambo oyo osengeli kotalela ntango ozali kosolola na monganga na yo mpo na kotoka na yo:

Koloba solo ezali malamu mingi: Atako ekoki kozala mpasi kosolola makambo mosusu, monganga na yo azali na mposa ya koyeba bilembo na yo nyonso, ata mpe ntango nini mpe esika nini otokaka mingi, biloko nini esalaka ete otoka, mpe ndenge nini yango ebebisaka bomoi na yo ya mokolo na mokolo. Makambo oyo esalisaka bango bayeba ntina ya bokono na yo mpe bapesa yo bankisi oyo ebongi na yo.

Ndenge ya kofanda ezali na ntina: Mimeseno na yo ya mokolo na mokolo, ata mpe biloko olyaka, ngalasisi, mpe mitungisi, ekoki kosala ete otoka mingi. Lobá polele ndenge ofandaka, mpo ntango mosusu kobongola mwa makambo ekoki kosala bokeseni monene.

Kobanga te kolobela mitungisi na yo: Soki ozali na mitungisi to mituna mpo na bankisi to mabe na yango, kobanga te kolobela yango. Monganga na yo azali wana mpo na koyanola na mituna na yo mpe kosala elongo na yo mpo na kozwa lisalisi oyo ebongi na bamposa mpe bolingo na yo.

Kobosanaka te, ozali yo moko te: Hyperhidrosis ezali bokono oyo ezwaka bato mingi. Koyebisa monganga na yo makambo okutanaka na yango mpe mitungisi na yo ekoki kosalisa yo oyeba kopekisa kotoka na yo mpe obongisa bomoi na yo.

Tolendisi yo ozwa bokutani mosusu na Dr. Anika Sharma mpo na kosolola mpo na mbano ya labo na yo ya sika mpe mitungisi mosusu nyonso oyo okoki kozala na yango. Elongo, tokoki kosala mpo na kozwa makambo ya malamu mpe kosalisa yo oyoka malamu mingi.

srcs: Hair Loss: A Common and Manageable Condition

Hair loss is a common concern for many people, including women. It can be caused by a variety of factors, including workplace injuries, stress, hormonal changes, and nutritional deficiencies. While hair loss can be distressing, it is often temporary and treatable.
Causes of Hair Loss After a Workplace Injury

In some cases, hair loss can occur after a workplace injury. This may be due to the physical trauma of the injury itself, or it could be a result of the stress and anxiety associated with the injury. Additionally, certain medications used to treat pain or inflammation may also contribute to hair loss.
Treatment Options

The treatment for hair loss will depend on the underlying cause. If your hair loss is related to stress or anxiety, finding ways to manage these emotions may help. This could involve techniques such as relaxation exercises, yoga, or meditation. If your hair loss is due to a nutritional deficiency, your doctor may recommend dietary changes or supplements.
Reassurance

It is important to remember that hair loss is often a temporary condition. With proper treatment and care, your hair is likely to grow back. If you are concerned about your hair loss, please do not hesitate to talk to your doctor. They can help you determine the cause of your hair loss and recommend the best course of treatment.
Additional Tips
Be gentle with your hair. Avoid harsh brushing or styling, and use a mild shampoo and conditioner.
Eat a healthy diet. Make sure you are getting enough protein, iron, and other nutrients that are important for hair health.
Manage stress. Find healthy ways to cope with stress, such as exercise, relaxation techniques, or spending time with loved ones.
Be patient. It takes time for hair to grow back. Do not get discouraged if you do not see results immediately.
Remember, you are not alone. Many women experience hair loss at some point in their lives. With the right support and treatment, you can manage your hair loss and regain your confidence.
trgs: Kokweyisama ya Suki: Maladi Moko oyo ezwaka Bato Mingi mpe Ekoki Kosalisama.

Kokweisama ya suki ezali likambo moko oyo epesaka bato mingi mitungisi, mingimingi epai ya basi. Ekoki kouta na makambo ndenge na ndenge, lokola kozoka na esika ya mosala, mitungisi ya makanisi, mbongwana na nzoto, mpe kozanga bilei ya malamu na nzoto. Atako kokweisa suki ekoki kopesa mpasi na motema, ezalaka mbala mingi ya ntango moke mpe ekoki kosalisama.
Ntina ya Kokeisama ya Suki Nsima ya Kozoka na Mosala

Na bantangu mosusu, kokweyisa suki ekoki kosalema nsima ya kozoka na mosala. Ekoki kozala mpo na mpasi ya nzoto ya kozoka yango moko, to ekoki kozala mpo na mitungisi ya makanisi mpe kobanga oyo eyaka na kozoka. Kutu, bankisi mosusu oyo basalelaka mpo na kosilisa mpasi to kovimba ekoki mpe kosala ete suki ekweya.
Ndenge ya Kozwa lobiko

Lobiko ya kokweyisama ya suki elandaka ntina na yango. Soki eutaka na mitungisi ya makanisi to kobanga, koluka koyeba ndenge ya koyanola na mayoki wana ekoki kosalisa. Ekoki kozala na nzela ya ba tekiniki neti bangalasisi ya kopema malamu, yoga, to komanyola. Soki euti na kozanga bilei ya malamu na nzoto, monganga na yo akoki kobongola bilei oyo okobanda kolya to bilei mosusu ya kobakisa.
Kolendisa

Ezali na ntina kobmikundola ete kokweyisa suki ezalaka mbala mingi likambo ya ntango moke. Na nzela ya lobiko mpe bozwi likebi ya malamu, suki na yo ekoki kokola lisusu. Soki ozali na mitungisi mpo na kobungisa suki na yo, tobondeli yo osolola na monganga na yo. Akoki kosalisa yo koyeba ntina ya kokweyisama ya suki na yo mpe kopesa yo toli ya lobiko oyo eleki malamu.
Batoli Mosusu
Kipé suki na yo. Boya kosanola yango to kokanga suki na makasi, mpe salela sabuni ya kosukola suki mpe kokawusa yango na boboto.
Lya bilei ya malamu. Sala ete olyaka ba proteine ya kokoka, fer, mpe bavitamini mosusu oyo ezali na ntina mpo na kolongono ya suki.
Yangela mitungisi ya makanisi. Luka ndenge ya malamu ya koyangela mitungisi ya makanisi, lokola kosala bangalasisi, ba teckiniki ya kopema, to kolekisa ntango na bato oyo olingaka.
Zala na motema molai. Esengaka ntango mpo suki ekola lisusu. Kolɛmba nzoto te soki omoni bambano ya mbala moko te.

Kobosana te, ozali yo moko te. Basi mingi bakutanaka na kokweyisama ya suki na ntango moko boye na bomoi na bango. Na lisalisi mpe lobiko ya malamu, okoki koyangela na kokweyisama ya suki na yo mpe kobanda komindima yo moko.

srcs: My name's Nikolai Petrovich, and I work security. Look, I don't have time for games. My family, yeah, they've got this thing, Shwachman-Diamond syndrome. Messes with their blood, their pancreas, whole lot of stuff. I haven't been feeling right lately, either. Tired all the time, can't shake a cold, stomach's been acting up.

It started a few weeks back. Just felt... off. Dragging myself through shifts, catching every bug going around. Thought maybe I was just run down, you know? But then the stomach issues started. Greasy, foul-smelling stuff, if you catch my drift. And the bruising... I barely bump into anything and I look like I've been in a fight.

My cousin, Dmitri, he's got it bad. Always sick, in and out of the hospital. Short for his age, too. My aunt says it's genetic. Something about bone marrow not working right, not making enough white blood cells to fight infection. And the pancreas not making enzymes to digest food properly. That explains the stomach problems, I guess.

So here I am. Figured I better get checked out before I end up like Dmitri. I need to know if I've got this thing, and if so, what we're gonna do about it. I got a job to do, people depending on me. Can't be calling in sick every other day. Just give it to me straight, doc. What are my chances?
trgs: Kombo na ngai Nikolai Petrovich, mpe nasalaka mosala ya kokengela. Yoka, nazali na ntango ya kolekisa te. Libota na ngai, ɛɛ, bazali na maladi oyo, maladi ya Shwachman-Diamond. Ebebisaka makila na bango, yéka na bango, mpe makambo mingi. Ngai mpe nazali komiyoka malamu te mikolo oyo. Nazali ya kolemba ntango nyonso, nazali kokoka te kolongola maladi ya miyoyo, nazali mikakatano na likundu.

Ebandaki mwa baposo eleki. Nazalaki kaka komiyoka... mabe. Nazalaki komibenda nzoto na mosala, kozwa maladi nyonso oyo ezali koleka. Nakanisaki mbala mosusu ezali kaka kolemba ya mpamba, oyebi? Kasi na nsima, mikakatano ya likundu ebandaki. Biloko ya mafuta, ya nsolo mabe, soki olimboli oyo nalingi koloba. Mpe bapota... nazali kotutana mpenza na eloko te kasi nazali komonana lokola nde nabundaki.

Ndeko na ngai, Dmitri, azali na yango makasi. Azali kobela ntango nyonso, kokende mpe kozonga na lopitalo. Azali mpe mokuse na kolanda mbula na ye. Tata-mwasi na ngai alobi ete ezalaka ya libota. Eloko moko oyo etali libúbu oyo ezali kosala malamu te, ezali kobota malamu te baselile ya mpembe na makila mpo na kobundisa maladi. Mpe yéke ezali kosala baanzyme te mpo na kosala boyangeli malamu ya bilei. Nakanisi yango nde elimboli mikakatano na ngai ya likundu.

Yango wana nazali awa. Namilobeli ete ezali malamu namitalisa liboso ete nakóma lokola Dmitri. Nazali na mposa ya koyeba soki nazali na bokono yango, mpe soki ezali bongo, tokoki kosala nini mpo na yango. Nazali na mosala ya kosala, bato bazali kotyela ngai motema. Nakoki te kobelabela mikolo nyonso. Yebisa ngai kaka bosolo, monganga. Matomba na ngai ezali nini?

srcs: Mr. Silas Hawthorne, a 52-year-old electrician, presented to the emergency department for a biopsy of a suspicious lesion on his right forearm. He reported noticing the lesion several weeks ago but initially dismissed it as a minor scrape from work. However, the lesion has since grown in size and become increasingly painful, prompting him to seek medical attention.

Upon examination, the lesion appeared as an ulcerated nodule with irregular borders and surrounding erythema. Mr. Hawthorne denied any history of skin cancer or significant sun exposure. He also reported no other symptoms such as fever, chills, or weight loss.

Given the concerning appearance of the lesion, a punch biopsy was performed under local anesthesia. The procedure was well-tolerated, and Mr. Hawthorne was discharged with instructions for wound care and follow-up with dermatology for results.
The biopsy specimen was sent to pathology for evaluation. The results are pending.
trgs: Mr. Silas Hawthorne, Mosali ya lotiliki ya mbula 52, ayaki na departema ya lobiko ya lobangu mpo na bolongoli misuni ya pota moko oyo ezali kopesa ntembe na loboko na ye ya mobali. Alobaki ete amonaki pota yango pɔsɔ mingi eleki kasi na ebandeli akanisaki ete ezalaki pota ya moke oyo azwaki na mosala. Kasi, pota yango ekomi monene mpe ezali kosala mpasi mingi, yango nde etindi ye aluka lisungi ya monganga.

Na ntango ya ekzame, pota yango ezalaki lokola nodule ya pota oyo ezali na bandelo ya mabe mpe na erytheme na zingazinga. M. Hawthorne alobaki ete atikala kobela kanser ya loposo te to atambolaki mingi na moi te. Alobaki mpe ete azalaki na bilembo mosusu te lokola fefele, malili, to kokita kilo.

Lokola pota yango ezalaki kopesa mitungisi, basalaki ye bolongoli misuni na punch na nse ya anesthésie locale. Procedure yango elekaki malamu, mpe M. Hawthorne abimaki na malako mpo na kobatela mpota mpe kozwa boukutani ya bolandeli ya makambo ya loposo mpo na koyeba mbano.
Ndakisa moko ya bolongoli misuni etindamaki na pathologie mpo na botaleli. Mbano ezali kozelama.

srcs: My name is Gisela Krueger, and I work as a mail carrier. I'm writing this down because I need a second opinion about these polyps. I've been feeling really anxious and frustrated, but I'm trying to stay calm. It started with a little bleeding, nothing major, but it's been happening more often lately. My doctor said it's probably just hemorrhoids, but I'm not so sure. Sometimes it feels like there's something blocking me up inside, and it's uncomfortable. I've also noticed some changes in my bowel movements, like they're narrower than usual. It's worrying me, especially since I spend so much time walking on my route. I'm hoping seeing a specialist will give me some answers and peace of mind. I just want to know what's going on and get the right treatment so I can get back to my normal life. Maybe it's nothing serious, but I'd rather be safe than sorry. I'm tired of worrying about this every day. I just need someone to listen to me and take my concerns seriously.
trgs: Kombo na ngai ezali Gisela Krueger, mpe nazali kosala mosala ya kokaba mikanda na posita. Nazali kokoma likambo oyo mpo nazali na mposa ya kozwa makanisi ya moto mosusu mpo na ba polype oyo. Nazali komiyoka mpenza na mitungisi mpe nkanda, kasi nazali komeka kozala kimia. Ebandaki na mwa makila moke, likambo ya monene te, kasi ezali kosalema mingi mikolo oyo. Dokotolo na ngai alobaki ete ekoki kozala kaka ba hemoroide, kasi nazali na ntembe. Ntango mosusu nayokaka neti ezali na eloko moko ekangi ngai na kati, mpe ezali kotungisa. Namoni mpe mwa mbongwana na ndenge na ngai ya kokende na toaleti, neti nde kaka ezali moke koleka ndenge ezalaka. Ezali kotungisa ngai, mingimingi mpo nalekisaka ntango mingi na kotambola na nzela na ngai. Nazali na elikya ete kokutana na specialist ekopesa ngai biyano mpe kimia ya makanisi. Nalingi kaka koyeba nini ezali kosalema mpe kozwa lisalisi oyo ebongi mpo nazonga na bomoi na ngai ya ndenge ezalaka. Mbala mosusu ezali likambo ya monene te, kasi nalingi nde kozala na kimia na esika ya komilela. Nalembi komitungisa na likambo oyo mokolo na mokolo. Nazali na mposa ya moto ayoka ngai mpe azwa mitungisi na ngai na makasi.

srcs: "Hello, this is Swee Lan Lim, a medical student. I understand you're looking for some information about an arterial biopsy?"
"That's correct, Swee. My name is Kavita Singh, and I'm a librarian. I've been having some concerning symptoms lately, and my doctor suggested I look into getting a biopsy."
"Okay, Kavita. Can you tell me a little bit more about what's been going on? What kind of symptoms have you been experiencing?"

"Well, I've been having some numbness and tingling in my hands and feet, and sometimes my fingers turn white or blue when I'm cold. My doctor mentioned something called vasculitis, and said an arterial biopsy could help confirm the diagnosis."

"That sounds like Raynaud's phenomenon, which can sometimes be associated with vasculitis. An arterial biopsy involves taking a small sample of tissue from an artery, usually the temporal artery on the side of your head, to look for inflammation under a microscope."
"Is it a painful procedure? Will I need to stay in the hospital?"

"It's generally a minor procedure performed under local anesthesia, so you shouldn't feel much pain during the biopsy itself. You might have some soreness afterwards, but over-the-counter pain medication should help. It's usually done as an outpatient procedure, so you'll likely be able to go home the same day."
"That's a relief. Are there any risks involved?"

"As with any procedure, there are some risks, such as bleeding, infection, or nerve damage, but these are rare. Your doctor will discuss the risks and benefits with you in more detail before the procedure."
"Okay, that sounds reasonable. How do I go about scheduling the biopsy?"

"Since this is a telehealth service, I can help you connect with a specialist who performs arterial biopsies. We can schedule a consultation for you to discuss the procedure further and answer any other questions you may have. Would you like me to do that for you?"
"Yes, please. That would be very helpful."
"Great. Let me get some information from you, and we'll get that set up."
trgs: "Mbote, nazali Swee Lan Lim, moyekoli na kelasi ya minganga. Nabanzi ete bozali koluka kozwa bansango mpo na biopisie ya ya misisa?"

"Ezali bongo, Swee. Kombo na ngai Kavita Singh, mpe nasalaka na biblioteke. Nazalaki koyoka mwa bilembo ya kobangisa na mikolo mileki, mpe monganga na ngai alobaki ete naluka kosala bolongoli ya ndambu ya mosuni."
"Malamu, Kavita. Okoki koyebisa nga mwa moke makambo oyo ezali kosalema? Okutanaki na bilembo nini?"

"Nazali koyoka nzoto kolemba mpe koswa na maboko mpe na makolo, mpe na bantango mosusu misapi na ngai ekomaka mpembe to ble soki nazali koyoka malili. Monganga na ngai alobelaki eloko moko babengi vaskilarité, mpe alobaki ete bolongoli misuni ekoki kosalisa mpo na koyebanisa maladi yango."

"Yango ezali lokola fenomene ya Raynaud, oyo na bantango mosusu ekoki kokokisama na vaskilarité. Bolongoli misuni esengaka kozwa mwa eteni moke ya mosuni na nzoto, mbala mingi mosuni ya monene oyo ezalaka mopanzi ya motó na yo, mpo na koluka kovimba moko na mikroskope."
"Kosalisa yango esalaka mpasi? Ekosenga ngai natikala na lopitalo?"

"Mbala mingi ezalaka kaka likambo ya moke oyo basalaka na nse ya anastézi ya mboka, yango wana okoyoka mpasi mingi te ntango bazali kosala bolingoli ya misuni yango. Okoki kozala na mwa mpasi na nsima, kasi bankisi ya kosilisa mpasi oyo batɛkaka na farmasi ekoki kosunga yo. Mbala mingi basalaka yango na kozanga kolala na lopitalo, yango wana mbala mosusu okoki kozonga na ndako mokolo yango kaka."
"Ezali kopesa ngai kimya. Ezalaka na makama?"

"Ndenge moko na mosala nyonso, ezalaka na mwa makama, lokola kobima makila, bokono, to kozoka na misisa, kasi makambo yango ekomaka mpenza te. Monganga na yo akolobela yo oyo etali makama mpe matomba na yango malamumalamu liboso ya kosala yango."
"Malamu, ezali komonana malamu. Ndenge nini nakoki kosala mpo na kozwa programe ya bolongoli misuni?"

"Lokola ezali kozwa lisungi ya monganga na mosika, nakoki kosalisa yo okutana na nganga-buka oyo asalaka bolongoli misuni. Tokoki kozwela yo bokutani mpo botalela lisusu likambo yango mpe ayanola yo na mituna mosusu oyo okoki kozala na yango. Olingi nasala yango mpo na yo?"
"Ee, palado. Ekosalisa penza."
"Malamu. Tiká nazwa mwa sango epai na yo, mpe tokobongisa yango."

srcs: Good morning, Hanna! It's wonderful to meet you. I understand you're here for the clinical trial screening related to food allergies. That's fantastic! Participating in research like this is incredibly valuable. It helps us understand allergies better and potentially develop new treatments that could benefit so many people, including yourself.

I know the idea of a clinical trial can sometimes feel a bit daunting, but please know that your safety and well-being are our top priorities throughout the entire process. The screening today is just the first step, and it's a great opportunity for you to learn more about the study and ask any questions you might have.

Remember, you're not just a participant; you're a partner in this journey towards better health. Your contribution could make a real difference in the lives of others facing similar challenges. So take a deep breath, relax, and let's get started. We're here to support you every step of the way. Do you have any questions before we begin? We're so glad you're here, Hanna. Let's do this together!
trgs: Mbote, Hanna! Ezali esengo komona yo. Nayoki ete oye mpo na botaleli ya boyekoli ya maladi etali bopekisi ya bilei. Ezali malamu mpenza! Kosangana na boyekoli ya ndenge wana ezali na ntina mingi. Esalisaka biso na koyeba malamu bipekiseli mpe kosala bankisi ya sika oyo ekoki kosunga bato mingi, ata mpe yo moko.

Nayebi ete likanisi ya kosangana na boyekoli ya maladi ekoki kopesa mwa bobangi, kasi yeba ete libateli mpe bolamu na yo nde ekozwa esika ya liboso na ntango nyonso ya mosala oyo. Botaleli ya lelo ezali kaka etambe ya liboso, mpe ezali libaku ya malamu mpo na yo oyeba makambo mingi etali boyekoli mpe otuna mituna nyonso oyo okoki kozala na yango.

Yeba ete, ozali kaka moto oyo azali kosangana na boyekoli te; ozali moninga na biso na mobembo oyo ya koluka lobiko ya malamu. Lisungi na yo ekoki kobongisa mpenza bomoi ya bato mosusu oyo bazali na mikakatano ndenge moko na yo. Yango wana pema makasi, fanda kimia, mpe tobanda. Tozali awa mpo na kosunga yo na etambe nyonso. Ozali na mituna liboso tobanda? Tozali na esengo mingi ndenge oye, Hanna. Tosala yango elongo!

srcs: Attending Physician (Dr. Shreya Patel): Okay, so the patient is a 67-year-old female calling with concerns about worsening shortness of breath. Her name is Mrs. Elara Vance. Let's go through her history.

Resident (Dr. Ravi Kapoor): Alright, Mrs. Vance reports a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia. She's been taking lisinopril and atorvastatin for several years. Recently, she's noticed increasing difficulty breathing with exertion, like climbing stairs or walking uphill.
Dr. Dupont: Any other symptoms? Chest pain, palpitations, dizziness?
Dr. Kapoor: No chest pain, but she mentions occasional palpitations and some mild dizziness when standing up quickly. She also reports some swelling in her ankles towards the end of the day.
Dr. Dupont: Okay, let's check her vitals. What's her blood pressure and heart rate?
Dr. Kapoor: Her blood pressure is 145/90 mmHg, and her heart rate is 88 beats per minute. Oxygen saturation is 96% on room air.
Dr. Dupont: That blood pressure is a bit high, even with medication. And the ankle swelling could be a sign of fluid retention. Let's ask about her diet and salt intake.
Dr. Kapoor: She says she tries to eat healthy but admits to enjoying salty snacks occasionally. She hasn't been monitoring her salt intake closely.

Dr. Dupont: We should advise her on reducing salt intake and monitoring her weight daily. Sudden weight gain can indicate fluid retention. Also, let's schedule an echocardiogram to assess her heart function.
Dr. Kapoor: Should we adjust her medications?

Dr. Dupont: Not yet. Let's see the echocardiogram results first. We might need to increase her lisinopril dose or add a diuretic if there's evidence of heart failure. In the meantime, emphasize lifestyle modifications and close monitoring.
Dr. Kapoor: Understood. I'll explain everything to Mrs. Vance and schedule the echocardiogram.
Dr. Dupont: Good. Remember, early detection and management are key in preventing complications. Let me know when you have the results.
trgs: Monganga ya sika (Dr. Shreya Patel): Ok, mobeli azali mwasi ya mibu 67 azali kobenga mpo na mitungisi na ntina na kokatana mpema oyo ezali kobakisama. Kombo na ye Madame Elara Vance. Tótala lisolo na ye ya kala na mae matali kolongono ya nzoto na ye.

Resident (Dr. Ravi Kapoor): Ok, Madame Vance alobi ete azalaka na tansyo ya likolo mpe hyperlipidémie. Amelaka nkisi ya lisinopril mpe atorvastatin na boumeli ya mibu mingi. Kala mingi te, amoni ete azali kokatana mpema mingi ntango azali kosala makasi, lokola komata na baeskalyé to kotambola na ngomba.
Dr. Dupont: Bilembo mosusu? Mpasi na ntolo, motema kobeta nokinoki, kizunguzungu?

Dr. Kapoor: Ayokaka mpasi na ntolo te, kasi alobeli motema kobeta nokinoki na bantango mosusu mpe mwa kizunguzungu soki atelemeli noki. Alobi mpe ete makolo na ye evimbaka mwa moke na nsuka ya mokolo.
Dr. Dupont: Ok, totalela binama na ye ya bomoi. Tansyo mpe vitesi ya motema na ye ezali boni?
Dr. Kapoor: Tansyo ya makila na ye ezali 145/90 mmHg, mpe vitesi ya motema na ye ezali 88 beats na miniti moko. Botongisami ya oxygène ezali 96% na libanda.
Dr. Dupont: Tansyo wana ezali mwa likolo, atako ameli nkisi. Mpe kovimba ya makolo ekoki kozala elembo ya kobomba mayi na nzoto. Tótuna ye mpo na bilei mpe mungwa oyo alyaka.
Dr. Kapoor: Alobi ete amekaka kolya malamu, kasi andimi ete alyaka biloko ya mungwa na bantango mosusu. Alandelaka penza te mungwa oyo alyaka.

Dr. Dupont: Tosengeli kopesa ye toli mpo na kokitisa mungwa oyo alyaka mpe kolandela kilo na ye mokolo na mokolo. Kobakisama ya kilo na mbalakaka ekoki komonisa kobomba mayi na nzoto. Lisusu, tóbongisa echocardiographi mpo na kotala ndenge motema na ye ezali kosala.
Dr. Kapoor: Tosengeli kobongola bankisi na ye?

Dr. Dupont: Naino te. Tótala naino mbano ya echocardiographi. Tokoki kosengela kobakisa doze na ye ya lisinopril to kobakisa nkisi oyo esubisaka soki ezali kolakisa elembo moko ya maladi ya motema. Na ntango oyo, tolobela mingi mbongwana ya lolenge ya bomoi mpe komilandela penepene.
Dr. Kapoor: Nayoki. Nakolimbola nyonso na Madame Vance mpe nakobongisa echocardiographi.
Dr. Dupont: Malamu. Kobosana te ete, koyeba noki mpe boyangeli ezali fungola mpo na kopekisa mikakatano. Yebisa ngai ntango okozwa mbano.

srcs: Dr. Nguyen,

My fingers feel clumsy too, like they don't want to cooperate when I'm trying to do delicate tasks like pinning boutonnieres or tying ribbons on favors. I've even noticed that the muscles in my hand look a bit smaller, like they're shrinking. It's really starting to affect my work, and you know how important it is for everything to be perfect on a wedding day! I'm worried I won't be able to keep up with the demands of my job if this keeps happening. Is there anything you can do to help me get my hand back to normal? I have three weddings coming up next month and I need to be at my best!
Sincerely,
Seraphina Sterling

srcs: Patient Instructions for Cold Sores
Avoid touching or scratching the cold sore.
Apply a cold compress to the affected area to reduce pain and swelling.
Keep the cold sore clean and dry.
Avoid sharing utensils, towels, or other personal items with others to prevent spreading the virus.
Take over-the-counter pain relievers, such as ibuprofen or acetaminophen, to manage pain.
Use a lip balm with sunscreen to protect the lips from sun exposure, which can trigger outbreaks.
Avoid kissing or intimate contact until the cold sore has completely healed.
Maintain good hygiene, including frequent handwashing.
Drink plenty of fluids to stay hydrated.
Monitor for signs of infection, such as increased redness, swelling, or pus.
Follow up with a healthcare provider if the cold sore does not improve or worsens.
If prescribed antiviral medication:
Take the medication as directed by your healthcare provider.
Complete the full course of medication, even if symptoms improve.
Be aware of potential side effects and contact your healthcare provider if they occur.
Important Note:
Cold sores are contagious. Take precautions to prevent spreading the virus to others.
If you experience severe pain, difficulty eating or drinking, or if the cold sore spreads to other areas, seek medical attention immediately.

srcs: Dr. Roberto Gonzales: Good morning, I see you're here for a refill on your prescription, is that right?
Ms. Ophelia Sinclair: Yes, doctor, it's for my jaundice medication. I've been taking it for a while now, but I seem to have run out.
Dr. Roberto Gonzales: I understand. Can you tell me a little bit more about how you've been feeling lately? Have you noticed any changes in your symptoms since you started taking the medication?

Ms. Ophelia Sinclair: Well, to be honest, doctor, I haven't been feeling very well at all. My stomach has been hurting quite a bit, and I've been feeling very tired and weak. And my skin still looks quite yellow, don't you think?

Dr. Roberto Gonzales: I do see that your skin has a yellowish tint, Ms. Sinclair. And I'm sorry to hear about your stomach pain and fatigue. Those can be symptoms of jaundice, but they can also be signs of other underlying conditions. Have you noticed any other changes, perhaps in your appetite or digestion?
Ms. Ophelia Sinclair: Now that you mention it, I haven't had much of an appetite lately. And I've been feeling a bit nauseous after eating.

Dr. Roberto Gonzales: I see. It's important that we get to the bottom of what's causing your symptoms, Ms. Sinclair. While I can certainly refill your prescription for the jaundice medication, I would also like to schedule some further tests to rule out any other potential causes for your discomfort.
Ms. Ophelia Sinclair: Tests? What kind of tests?

Dr. Roberto Gonzales: We'll start with some blood work to check your liver function and bilirubin levels. Depending on the results, we may also need to do an ultrasound or other imaging tests to get a better look at your liver and gallbladder.
Ms. Ophelia Sinclair: Oh, I see. Is it serious, doctor?

Dr. Roberto Gonzales: It's too early to say for sure, Ms. Sinclair. But by running these tests, we can get a better understanding of what's going on and ensure that we're providing you with the most appropriate treatment.
Ms. Ophelia Sinclair: Alright, doctor. Whatever you think is best.

Dr. Roberto Gonzales: Thank you for your cooperation, Ms. Sinclair. I'll go ahead and write you a prescription for the refill, and my nurse will help you schedule the blood work. We'll get to the bottom of this together.
Ms. Ophelia Sinclair: Thank you, doctor. I appreciate your help.
trgs: Dr. Roberto Gonzales: Mbote, namoni oye kozua lisusu mokanda ya nkisi na yo, ezali bongo?
Ms. Ophelia Sinclair: Ee, monganga, ezali mpo na nkisi na ngai ya maladi ya jonise. Nazali komela yango banda mwa ntango, kasi emonani lokola esili.
Dr. Roberto Gonzales: Nayoki. Okoki koyebisa ngai mwa moke ndenge ozali komiyoka mikolo oyo? Omoni mbongwana ya bilembo na yo banda obandaki komela nkisi yango?

Ms. Ophelia Sinclair: Malamu, mpo na koloba solo, monganga, nazali komiyoka malamu ata moke te. Libumu na ngai ezali koswa ngai makasi penza mpe nazali koyoka bolembu mpe nazali na makasi te. Mpe loposo na ngai ezali langi ya mosaka, omoni yango te?

Dr. Roberto Gonzales: Namoni ete loposo na yo ezali na langi ya mosaka, Madame Sinclair. Mpe nayoki mawa mpo na mpasi ya libumu na yo mpe bolembu. Yango ekoki kozala bilembo ya jonise, kasi ekoki mpe kozala bilembo ya maladi mosusu. Omoni bambongwana misusu, na ndakisa na mae matali mposa na yo ya kolya to na ndenge ozali konika bilei?
Ms. Ophelia Sinclair: Lokola olobeli yango, nazali na mposa ya kolya mingi te mikolo oyo. Mpe motema ezali kobalukabaluka na nsima ya kolya.

Dr. Roberto Gonzales: Nayoki. Ezali na ntina ete toyeba nini ezali kopesa yo bilembo oyo, Madame Sinclair. Ata soki nakoki kopesa yo lisusu mokanda ya bankisi ya jonise, nalingi mpe osalisa baekzame mosusu mpo na koyeba kolongola ntina mosusu ya mpasi na yo.
Ms. Ophelia Sinclair: Baekzame? Baekzame ya ndenge nini?

Dr. Roberto Gonzales: Tokobanda na botaleli ya makila mpo na kotala ndenge libale na yo ezali kosala mpe nivo ya bilirubine. Na kolanda mbano, tokoki mpe kosala ekografi to baekzame misusu ya bililingi mpo na komona malamu libale na yo mpe mwa saki moke ya nsongi.
Ms. Ophelia Sinclair: Ah, nayoki. Ezali makasi, monganga?

Dr. Roberto Gonzales: Tozali naino na ebandeli penza mpo na kolobela yo yango na bosikisiki, Madame Sinclair. Kasi baekzame oyo, ekoki kosunga biso tozala na bososoli malamu ya makambo oyo ezali kosalema mpe kopesa lobiko oyo ebongi mpenza.
Ms. Ophelia Sinclair: Malamu, monganga. Nyonso oyo okanisi ezali malamu.

Dr. Roberto Gonzales: Matondi mpo na boyokani na yo, Madame Sinclair. Nakokomela yo mokanda ya bankisi ya komela lisusu, mpe lifulume na ngai akosalisa yo mpo na kokanga mokolo ya bokutani mpo na ekzame ya makila. Tokolonga likambo yango elongo.
Ms. Ophelia Sinclair: Matondi, monganga. Nasepeli mingi mpo na lisungi na yo.

srcs: Given your garrulous nature and family history of Bloom syndrome, understanding your situation is crucial. Bloom syndrome is a serious, inherited disorder characterized by significant growth delays, sun sensitivity, and an increased risk of various cancers. It's vital to be aware of the potential signs and symptoms, which include:
Severe sun sensitivity: Even brief sun exposure can lead to skin rashes and blisters.
Short stature: Individuals with Bloom syndrome typically experience significant growth delays.
Distinctive facial features: A long, narrow face with a small jaw and prominent nose is often characteristic.
Increased cancer risk: Bloom syndrome significantly increases the risk of developing various cancers, including leukemia, lymphoma, and solid tumors.
Recurrent infections: Due to a weakened immune system, individuals with Bloom syndrome may be more susceptible to infections.
Learning difficulties: Some individuals may experience learning difficulties or intellectual disabilities.
Given these potential complications, it's imperative to adhere to the following instructions:
Strict sun protection: Avoid direct sun exposure as much as possible. Wear protective clothing, hats, and sunglasses, and apply sunscreen liberally.
Regular medical checkups: Schedule regular appointments with your doctor to monitor growth, development, and overall health.
Cancer screening: Discuss appropriate cancer screening protocols with your doctor, considering your increased risk.
Genetic counseling: Consult a genetic counselor to understand the inheritance pattern of Bloom syndrome and its implications for your family.
Support groups: Connect with support groups or organizations dedicated to Bloom syndrome for information and emotional support.

Remember, while Bloom syndrome presents challenges, early diagnosis and management can significantly improve outcomes. By following these instructions and working closely with your healthcare team, you can navigate this condition effectively.
Dr. Xylia Zhang
Emergency Department Physician
St. Jude's Hospital
trgs: Na kolanda ezalela na yo ya koloba mingi mpe lisolo ya libota na yo mpo na maladi ya Bloom, kososola ezalela na yo ezali na ntina. Maladi ya Bloom ezali maladi monene oyo basangolaka, bilembo na yango ezalaka kozanga kokola malamu, komiyoka mabe na moi mpe bakanser ya ndenge na ndenge. Ezali likambo ya ntina koyeba bilembo mpe bimoniseli oyo ekoki kozala:
Komiyoka mabe makasi na moi: Ata kotikala na nse ya moi mpo na mwa ntangu moke ekoki kopesa mpasi na loposo mpe maputu.
Kozala mokuse: Bato oyo bazalaka na maladi ya Bloom mbala mingi bakolaka na lobangu te.
Bilembo ya kokesenisa elongi: Elongi ya molai mpe moke, na mbanga ya moke mpe zolo ya monene ezalaka mbala mingi bilembo.
Likama monene ya kozwa kanser: Maladi ya Bloom ematisaka mingi likama ya kozwa bakanser ya ndenge na ndenge, lokola lesemi, limfoma, mpe ba mbuma ya makasi.
Mikrobe ya mbala na mbala: Lokola ebongiseli oyo ebatelaka nzoto ezali na bolembu, bato oyo bazali na maladi ya Bloom bakoki kozwa mikrobe nokinoki.
Mikakatano ya koyekola: Bato mosusu bakoki kozala na mikakatano ya koyekola tokozala bozoba.
Na kolanda mikakatano oyo ekoki kozala, ezali na ntina mingi kolanda malako oyo elandi:
Komibatela makasi na moi: Kokima kotikala na nse ya moi. Lata bilamba ya komibatela, ekoti mpe maneti ya moi, mpe pakola kreme ya moi ebele.
Kozongela monganga mbala na mbala: Zongelaka monganga na yo mbala na mbala mpo na kolandela bokoli, botomboli, mpe kolongono ya nzoto mobimba.
Kotala kanser: Solola na monganga na yo mae matali ba ndenge ya kotalela kanser oyo ebongi, na kolanda likama na yo ya monene.
Toli ya genetike: Solola na mopesi-toli ya genetike mpo na kososola ndenge maladi ya Bloom epanzanaka mpe ntina na yango mpo na libota na yo.
Bituluku ya lisungi: Solola na bituluku ya lisungi to ba bibongiseli oyo etalelaka maladi ya Bloom mpo na kozwa bansango mpe lisungi ya mayoki.

Kobosana te, atako maladi ya Bloom ezali na mikakatano, koyeba yango noki mpe kobongama mpo na yango ekoki kobongisa makambo. Na kolanda malako oyo mpe na kosala na boyokani na ekipi na yo ya baminganga, okoki kolonga ezalela oyo malamu.
Dr. MoXylia Zhang
Monganga ya Departema ya mbalakaka

srcs: The patient, Aris Thorne, a 28-year-old transgender man currently 26 weeks pregnant, presents with noticeable anxiety regarding recent laboratory findings indicating hypoglycemia. Aris has a complex medical history, including managed type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and a previous diagnosis of polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) prior to his transition. Despite diligent adherence to his prenatal care plan and medication regimen, his blood sugar levels have dropped unexpectedly, causing him significant distress. He expresses concern not only for his own health but also for the potential impact on the developing fetus. Aris appears visibly fatigued and worried, frequently adjusting his posture and seeking reassurance about the implications of these results. His anxiety is compounded by the challenges of managing multiple chronic conditions alongside his pregnancy. The consultation requires a sensitive and comprehensive approach to address his fears, review his current treatment plan, and establish a strategy to stabilize his blood sugar levels while ensuring the safety and well-being of both Aris and his pregnancy.
trgs: Mobeli, Aris Thorne, mobali moko oyo abongwana mwasi ya mibu 28 oyo azali sikoyo na zemi ya baposo 26, amonisi mitungisi ya makasi mpo na mbano ya labo ya kala mingi te oyo emonisi kotambola malembe ya makila. Aris azali na lisolo ya makambo ya kolongono ya nzoto ya mindondo, ata mpe diabeti ya tynivo 2 oyo elandelami, tansyo ya likolo, mpe bokono ya ovaire polycystique (PCOS) liboso ya transition na ye. Atako atosi na likebi myango na ye ya lisalisi ya bokengi mpe bokambami ya nkisi, ba nivo ya sukali na ye ya makila ekiti kozanga kozela, kopesaka ye mpasi makasi. Amonisi mitungisi kaka mpo na kolongono ya nzoto na ye moko te kasi mpe mpo na bopusi oyo ekoki kozala na mwana oyo azali kokola. Aris amonani polele alembi mpe azali komitungisa, mbala mingi azali kobongisa etelelelo na ye mpe koluka kozwa elikya mpo na ntina ya ba resultats oyo. Mitungisi na ye ebakisami na mikakatano ya kolandela bamaladi ya kronike ebele nzela moko na zemi na ye. Bokutani esengeli na lolenge ya mayele mpe ya mobimba mpo na kotalela kobanga na ye, kotalela lisusu myango na ye ya traitema ya sikoyo, mpe kotia stratezi mpo na kotelemisa ba nivo ya sukali na ye ya makila ntango azali kosala ete bokengi mpe bolamu ya Aris mpe zemi na ye ezala.

srcs: I'm Pape Gueye, and I feel ridiculous. I'm seventy-four years old, my knees creak when I stand up, and I'm here for a sports physical. Not for pickleball, not for shuffleboard, but for competitive ballroom dancing. My partner, Mrs. Gupta - Maya - insists we enter the regional championships. She's a firecracker, that one, barely five feet tall and overflowing with energy. I, on the other hand, am built like a dried twig, liable to snap in a strong breeze.

The waiting room is a symphony of coughs and crying children. I perch on the edge of a plastic chair, clutching the paperwork Maya filled out for me. "History of heart murmur," it says. "Slight tremor in hands." I try to hide the tremor by gripping the papers tighter. A nurse calls my name, "Pape Gueye?" She's young, with bright eyes and a kind smile.
"That's me," I say, pushing myself up. My knees pop audibly.
"Right this way, Mr. Gueye."

She leads me to an exam room, takes my vitals, asks about my medications. I rattle off the list - blood pressure, cholesterol, something for the tremor. She nods, typing away on her computer. Then the doctor comes in. Dr. Fassi. He's a tall man with a gentle voice and hands that feel surprisingly warm when he checks my pulse.
"So, ballroom dancing?" he asks, raising an eyebrow.
"My partner is very persuasive," I admit.

He listens to my heart, checks my reflexes, makes me walk back and forth across the small room. I try to stand tall, to move with some semblance of grace. He doesn't say anything, just hums thoughtfully. Finally, he sits down on his stool and looks at me.

"Mr. Gueye," he says, "your heart is a little irregular, and your balance isn't what it used to be. But..." He pauses, a small smile playing on his lips. "I see a spark in your eyes. And if Mrs. Gupta is anything like you describe her, I imagine she'll keep you on your toes. Literally."
He signs the form with a flourish. "You're cleared to dance, Dikembe. Just... take it easy on the dips, alright?"
I walk out of the exam room feeling lighter than I have in years. Maybe I am a dried twig, but even dried twigs can dance in the wind. And with Maya leading, I might just surprise myself.
trgs: Kombo na ngai Pape Gueye, mpe nazali komiyoka lokola zoba. Nazali na mibu ntuku nsambo na minei, mabolongo na ngai ezali kobeta makelele soki natelemi, mpe nazali awa mpo na komekama ya nzoto ya ngalasisi. Te mpo na pickleball, te mpo na shuffleboard, kasi mpo na momekano ya mabina ya ballroom. Moninga na ngai, Madame. Gupta - Maya - azali kopusa biso tokota na masano oyo ezali kosalema na etuka. Azali lokola moto ya moto, molayi moko ya bametele moko na ndambo, kasi atonda na nguya. Ngai, na ngambo mosusu, nazali lokola etambe ya nzete ekauka, oyo ekoki kobukana na mopepe makasi.

Ndako ya kozela ezali na makelele ya batu bazali kokosola mpe bana bazali kolela. Nafandi na nsonge ya kiti ya plastiki, nasimbi ba papyé oyo Maya atondisaki mpo na ngai. Bakomaki,"Lisolo ya kala ya bopemi na motema". "Kolenga muke na maboko." Nameki kobomba kolenga wana na kosimbaka ba papyé makasi. Lifulume moko abengi kombo na ngai, "Pape Gueye?" Azali elenge, na miso ya kongenga mpe na koseka ya malamu.
Nayanolaki na kotombola elongi, "Ezali ngai". Mabolongo na ngai ebeti makelele ya koyokana.
"Leka boye, Mr. Gueye."

Amemi ngai na ndako moko ya baekzame, ameki bilembo na ngai ya bomoi, atuni mpo na bankisi na ngai. Natangi liste na yango - tansyo, kolesterole, nkisi moko mpo na kolenga. Andimi na moto, misu kaka na ordinatere na ye. Na nsima monganga akoti. Dr. Fassi. Azali mobali molayi na mongongo ya malamu mpe maboko oyo ezali na molunge mwa mingi ntango amekaki bokasi na ngai ya bomoyi.
Atunaki na kotombola mankiki moko "Ebongo, mabina ya ballroom?"
Nandimi, "Moninga na ngai azali na nguya ya kondimisa ngai."

Ayoki motema na ngai, atali bajeste na ngai, atambwisi ngai bipayi na bipayi epai na mwa ndako ya muke. Nameki kotelema semba, kotambola na mwa ngolu. Alobi eloko te, kaka konyonyo, azali koknisa. Nsukansuka, afandi na ebonga na ye mpe atali ngai.

"Mr. Gueye," alobaki na ngai, "motema na yo ezali mabe, mpe bokatikati na yo ezali lisusu te ndenge ezalaka. Kasi..." Atelemi mwa moke, koseka muke na mbebo na ye. "Namoni mwa moto na miso na yo. Mpe soki Madame Gupta azali ndenge olimboleli ngai ye, nakanisi akomonisa yo mpasi. Ya solo penza."
Atyaki sinyatire na formilere na lombangu. "Opesami nzela ya kobina, Dikembe. Kaka... malembe na bamuvema ya mukongo na yo, ok?"

Nabimi na ndako ya ekzame nazali komiyoka pɛpɛlɛ koleka ndenge nazalaki na mibu mingi. Mbala mosusu nazali etambe ya nzete ekauka, kasi ata bitambe ya nzete bikauka ekoki kobina na mopepe. Mpe na bosungi ya Maya, nakoki komikamwisa ngai moko.

srcs: Operator: Hello, this is MediCall, my name is Anya Petrova. How can I help you today?
Patient: Hi Anya, my name is Leo Rossi. I'm feeling really nauseous and I don't know what to do.
Operator: It's okay, Leo. Nausea can be very uncomfortable, but we're here to help. Can you tell me a little more about what's been going on?
Patient: I woke up feeling sick to my stomach and it hasn't gone away. I tried drinking some water, but it just made me feel worse.
Operator: I understand. Have you eaten anything today?
Patient: No, I haven't been able to keep anything down.
Operator: Okay, that's understandable. Have you been experiencing any other symptoms, like vomiting or diarrhea?
Patient: No, just the nausea.
Operator: Alright. It sounds like you might be dehydrated. Have you been drinking enough fluids lately?
Patient: I think so, but I'm not sure.
Operator: That's okay. Let's start by trying to hydrate you. Can you sip on some clear fluids, like water or ginger ale?
Patient: I can try.
Operator: Great. Just take small sips and see how you feel. If you start to feel worse, stop drinking and call us back.
Patient: Okay, thank you.
Operator: You're welcome, Leo. We'll check back in with you in a little while to see how you're doing. In the meantime, try to rest and relax.
Patient: Okay, I will. Thank you again.
Operator: No problem. Take care, Leo.
trgs: Mosali: Mbote, ezali MediCall, kombo na ngai Anya Petrova. Lolenge nini nakoki kosalisa yo lelo?
Mobeli: Mbote Anya, kombo na ngai Leo Rossi. Nazali koyoka mposa ya kosanza mpe nayebi te eloko nini nakoki kosala.
Mosali: Malamu, Leo. Mposa ya kosanza ekoki kozala mabe makasi, kasi tozali awa mpo na kosunga yo. Okoki koloba na ngai mwa moke makambo oyo ezali koleka?
Mobeli: Nalamukaki na mposa ya kosanza mpe esili te. Namekaki komela mayi, kutu yango nde ebebisi lisusu makambu.
Mosali: Nayoki. Olyé eloko lelo?
Mobeli: Te, nakokaki kobomba eloko te.
Mosali: Ok, nayoki. Ozali koyoka bilembo mosusu, neti kosanza to koleka lubumu?
Mobeli: Te, kaka mposa ya kosanza.
Mosali: Ok. Emonani neti ozangi mayi na nzoto. Ozali komela biloko ya mayi mingi mikolo oyo?
Mobeli: Nakanisi bongo, kasi nayebi malamu penza te.
Mosali: Ezali malamu. Tobanda na kopesa yo mayi. Okoki komela ndambu ya biloko ya mayi ya polele, neti mayi to soda ya tangawisi?
Mobeli: Nakoki komeka.
Mosali: Malamu. Mela moke moke mpe tala ndenge okomiyoka. Soki obandi koyoka mabe, tika komela mpe benga biso lisusu.
Mobeli: Ok, matondi.
Mosali: Likambu te Leo. Tokobenga yo lisusu na nsima ya mwa ntangu mpo na koyeba nsango na yo. Kasi sikawa, meka kopema mpe kofanda kimia.
Mobeli: Ok, nakosala bongo. Matondi lisusu.
Mosali: Likambu te. Batela nzoto na yo, Leo.

srcs: Hey Doc, good to see ya! You know, the roads haven't been too kind lately. My lower back's been giving me grief after all those miles, and I've been getting these weird tingles in my left hand, especially when I grip the wheel for too long. Oh, and don't even get me started on the heartburn after a truck stop burger - feels like a volcano in my chest sometimes! But hey, gotta keep on trucking, right?
trgs: Mbote monganga, nasepeli komona yo ! Oyebi, banzela ezali malamu te mikolo oyo. Mukongo na ngai ya nse ezali kosala ngai mpasi nsima ya kotambola bakilometre nyonso wana, mpe nazali koyoka loboko na ngai ya mobali ezali koswa, mingimingi soki nazali kokumba ntango molayi. Ah, mpe kotuna ngai te mpo na likundu na ngai na nsima ya kolya amburgere ya esika batekaka esansi ezali lokola volcan na ntolo na ngai ntango mosusu! Kasi, esengeli kokoba kokumba, boye te?

srcs: My doctor says my pituitary gland, a tiny gland at the base of my brain, isn't working as it should. It's like the control center for other hormones in my body, so when it's off, things get a little haywire. That explains why I've been feeling so tired lately, and maybe even some of the weight gain and mood swings. It's not something to worry too much about though, because there are treatments available to help get my hormones back in balance. The doctor mentioned medication or sometimes even surgery, but we'll figure out the best plan together. It's good to finally have some answers and a path forward to feeling better.
trgs: Monganga na ngai alobi hypophyse na ngai, mwa mbuma moko oyo eazali na nse ya boongo, ezali kosala te ndenge esengeli. Ezali lokola esika ya bokengeli mpo na ba hormone na nzoto na ngai, yango wana soki esali te, makambo ebebi. Yango nde emonisi ntina nazalaki koyoka bolembu mingi mikolo oyo, mpe ntango mosusu komata na ngai ya kilo mpe kobongwana ya makanisi. Kasi ezali likambo ya komitungisa mingi te, mpo ezali na bankisi oyo ekoki kosalisa mpo na kobongisa ba hormone na ngai. Monganga alobaki mpo na nkisi to ntango mosusu ata lipaso, kasi tokomona elongo nini ekobonga malamu. Ezali malamu mpo nasilisi kozwa biyano mpe nzela ya kolanda mpo nayoka malamu.

srcs: Hello there, I'm [Student Name], a medical student working with the doctor today. I see you're here because you've been losing weight without trying. Can you tell me a bit more about that?
I understand this can be worrying. How much weight have you lost, and over what period of time?
Okay, that's helpful to know. Have you noticed any other changes in your health or how you've been feeling lately? For example, changes in appetite, energy levels, or sleep patterns?
Have you experienced any fever, night sweats, or coughing recently?
And have you had any changes in your bowel habits or noticed any blood in your stool?
Alright, thank you for sharing that. Now, I'd like to ask a few questions about your medical history. Have you ever been diagnosed with any chronic conditions like diabetes or thyroid problems?
Are you currently taking any medications, including over-the-counter drugs or supplements?
Okay, noted. Do you have any family history of significant illnesses, particularly cancers or autoimmune diseases?
And finally, can you tell me a bit about your lifestyle? Do you smoke, drink alcohol, or use any recreational drugs?

Thank you for being so open with me. I'm going to discuss everything we've talked about with the doctor, and we'll come back together to figure out the next steps. Is there anything else you'd like to mention or ask before I go?
